triples.relationship: lament over apparent divine delay amid oppression
triples.rationale: Habakkuk asks how long he must cry while wronged without being heard or saved. The psalm likewise repeatedly asks how long the Lord will turn away, then asks Him to hear lest the enemy prevail. Both voice distressed waiting for divine help.
triples.source_text: How long, Lord, shall I cry and Thou wilt not listen? I shall cry to Thee while being wronged, and Thou wilt not save?

target_units.text: How long, Lord, wilt Thou forget me utterly? How long wilt Thou turn Thy face away from me?
How long shall I place counsels within my soul, pains within my heart by day? How long will my enemy be raised above me?
Look; hear me, Lord my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I fall asleep into death,
lest my enemy say, “I prevailed against him.” Those who afflict me will exult if I am shaken.

triples.relationship: wrongdoing encountered in the place of judgment
triples.rationale: Habakkuk complains of misery and impiety, with judgment against him and a judge who takes. Ecclesiastes likewise observes an ungodly person in the place of judgment and righteousness. Both locate wrongdoing where justice should be administered.
triples.source_text: Why didst Thou show me toil and pain, to look upon misery and impiety? Judgment has come against me, and the judge takes.

target_units.text: Again I saw beneath the sun: in the place of judgment, the ungodly person was there; in the righteous person’s place, the ungodly person was there.

triples.relationship: judgment distorted or driven back
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes scattered law and distorted judgment while the impious oppresses the righteous. Isaiah likewise says judgment was driven backward, righteousness withdrew and the Lord was displeased at the absence of judgment. Both connect public injustice with the failure of judgment.
triples.source_text: Therefore law has been scattered, and judgment is not brought to completion; the impious oppresses the righteous, so judgment will go forth distorted.

target_units.text: We drove judgment backward, and righteousness has withdrawn far away, for truth was consumed in their ways, and they could not go straight through.
Truth has been taken away, and they turned their mind away from understanding. The Lord saw, and it did not please Him that there was no judgment.

triples.relationship: explicit later quotation of an unbelievable divine work
triples.rationale: Habakkuk addresses despisers and announces a work they will not believe even when recounted. Acts explicitly warns about what the prophets spoke and repeats the address, wonder and vanishing, and the work that will not be believed. The wording directly connects the warning.
triples.source_text: Look, you despisers, observe, marvel at wonders and vanish! For I am doing a work in your days that you will certainly not believe if someone recounts it.

target_units.text: Take care, then, lest what is spoken in the prophets come upon you:
‘Look, you scoffers, marvel and vanish, for I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe even if someone recounts it to you.’”

triples.relationship: the Lord brings an invading nation
triples.rationale: Habakkuk announces the Lord raising Chaldean warriors who seize dwellings not their own. Jeremiah likewise announces a distant nation brought against Israel to consume its produce and attack fortified cities. Both present the invading force within a divine announcement, without assigning Jeremiah Habakkuk's national label.
triples.source_text: For look, I am raising up against you the Chaldean warriors, the bitter and swift nation, who traverse the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not their own.

target_units.text: Behold, I am bringing a nation upon you from far away, house of Israel, says the Lord, a nation whose language’s sound you will not understand.
All are strong,

and they will devour your harvest and your bread, and devour your sons and daughters, and devour your sheep and calves, and devour your vineyards and fig orchards and olive groves; and with a sword they will thresh your fortified cities, in which you have trusted.

triples.relationship: an imperial force claims authority for itself
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes the invaders' judgment and claim proceeding from themselves. Isaiah quotes the Assyrian ruler crediting his own strength and wisdom for seizing nations without resistance. Both expose the conqueror's self-assertion, in distinct descriptions of imperial power.
triples.source_text: Fearsome and conspicuous are they; their judgment will come from themselves, and their claim will proceed from themselves.

target_units.text: For he said, “By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of understanding. I will remove nations’ boundaries, plunder their strength and shake inhabited cities.
I will seize the whole inhabited world in my hand like a nest, and lift it like abandoned eggs. There is no one who will escape me or contradict me.”

triples.relationship: a distant invading nation compared to an eagle
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes horsemen rushing from afar and flying like an eagle eager to eat. Deuteronomy likewise announces a nation from afar coming like an eagle's swoop. The distance and predatory flight imagery connect the threats.
triples.source_text: Their horses will leap beyond leopards and be fiercer than the wolves of Arabia. Their horsemen will ride out and rush from afar, flying like an eagle eager to eat.

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,

triples.relationship: the gathering of large numbers of captives
triples.rationale: Habakkuk pictures the invading force gathering captives like sand. Kings recounts Babylon's king deporting rulers, warriors and craftsmen in large stated numbers. The historical account illustrates mass deportation without equating its numerical totals with the sand comparison.
triples.source_text: An end will come upon the impious who stand facing them in opposition, and they will gather captives like sand.

target_units.text: He deported Jerusalem, all the rulers, and the mighty in strength, taking ten thousand captives, and every craftsman and one who shuts up. None remained except the land’s poor.
He deported Joakim to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, and his eunuchs. He led the land’s powerful men into deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon,
and all the men of the force, seven thousand, and the craftsmen and those who shut up, one thousand—all mighty men who waged war. The king of Babylon brought them into deportation to Babylon.

triples.relationship: siege works used against fortified cities
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says the invaders mock fortresses, throw up a mound and seize them. Ezekiel's oracle names Babylon's king and describes building around Tyre, enclosing it with a palisade and weapons, and throwing down its walls. Both portray siege construction overcoming defenses.
triples.source_text: They will revel among kings, and tyrants will be their toys; they will mock every fortress, throw up a mound and seize it.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord: I am bringing against you, Tyre, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north—he is king of kings—with horses, chariots, horsemen, and an assembly of very many nations.
He will kill your daughters in the plain with the sword, set an advance guard against you, build around you, and make a palisade and a ring of weapons around you; he will set his spears opposite you.
He will throw down your walls and your towers with his swords.

triples.relationship: same-book recognition of strength as God's
triples.rationale: Habakkuk 1:11 concludes that this strength belongs to the speaker's God. The final verse likewise calls the Lord God the speaker's strength. This explicit shared attribution is retained without changing 1:11's preceding spirit and propitiation wording.
triples.source_text: Then the spirit will change and pass through and make propitiation. This strength belongs to my God.

target_units.text: The Lord God is my strength; He will set my feet toward completion and lead me onto the heights, to conquer in His song.

triples.relationship: a hostile power appointed within divine judgment
triples.rationale: Habakkuk addresses the Lord as having appointed the threatening figure for judgment. Isaiah likewise calls Assyria a rod of divine anger, while distinguishing the ruler's destructive intention. The connection concerns the power's assigned role, not agreement with every purpose of the invader.
triples.source_text: Art Thou not from the beginning, Lord, my holy God? We shall certainly not die. Lord, Thou hast appointed him for judgment, and He formed me to reprove his discipline.

target_units.text: Woe to the Assyrians! The rod of My anger and wrath is in their hands.
I will send My anger against a lawless nation, and I will command My people to take spoils and plunder, trample the cities and reduce them to dust.
But he did not consider it this way and has not reckoned it this way in his soul; rather, his mind will turn aside, even to destroy not a few nations.

triples.relationship: the difficulty of wicked prosperity beside righteous suffering
triples.rationale: Habakkuk questions God's silence when the impious swallows the righteous. The psalm likewise places prosperous sinners beside the speaker's apparently vain righteousness and daily scourging. Both articulate the distress caused by the apparent advantage of the wicked.
triples.source_text: Thine eye is pure, not to see evil things, and Thou wilt not be able to look upon distress. Why dost Thou look upon despisers? Wilt Thou remain silent when the impious swallows the righteous?

target_units.text: Behold, these are sinners, and they prosper; for the age they took possession of wealth.
And I said, “Then in vain I made my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent;
and I became scourged all day, and my rebuke comes in the mornings.”

triples.relationship: people pictured as vulnerable fish
triples.rationale: Habakkuk likens people to fish without a leader, before describing their capture. Ecclesiastes likewise compares people caught by an evil time to fish in an evil net. Both use the vulnerability of fish to describe human exposure to harm.
triples.source_text: Thou wilt make people like the fish of the sea and like creeping things with no leader.

target_units.text: For a person does not know his time: like fish caught in an evil net, and birds caught in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly.

triples.relationship: the catching of people represented as fishing
triples.rationale: Habakkuk depicts a whole catch hauled by hook, casting net and seines, continuing the comparison of people with fish. Jeremiah likewise describes fishermen sent to fish for the people, followed by hunters and repayment for wrongdoing. Both apply fishing to the taking of people, with distinct agents and instruments.
triples.source_text: They hauled up an entire catch with a hook, dragged it in a casting net and gathered it in their seines; therefore they will rejoice and their heart will be glad.

target_units.text: Behold, I am sending the many fishermen, says the Lord, and they will fish for them; and after these things I will send the many hunters, and they will hunt them on every mountain and hill and from the rocks’ openings.
Because My eyes are upon all their ways, and their wrongdoings were not hidden before My eyes.
And I will repay double their injustices and sins, for which they profaned My land with the corpses of their abominations and with their lawless acts, by which they offended against My inheritance.

triples.relationship: worship directed to material things associated with food and benefit
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says the captors sacrifice to nets because these provide their rich food. Isaiah describes wood used for warmth and cooking, with the rest fashioned into a god and worshiped. Both expose worship directed toward material means of benefit, while the actions upon the material differ.
triples.source_text: Therefore they will sacrifice to their seine and burn incense to their casting net, for through them they fattened their portion, and their foods are choice.

target_units.text: so that it might serve people for burning. Taking some, he warmed himself; after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. They worked the rest into gods and worship them.

Half of it they burned in fire, and after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. Over it he roasted meat, ate, and was satisfied. Warmed, he said, ‘It is pleasant for me, for I am warm and have seen fire!’
He made the rest into a carved god and worships it and prays, saying, ‘Rescue me, for you are my god.’

triples.relationship: same-book accusation of destructive action against nations and its consequence
triples.rationale: Habakkuk 1:17 describes continuing to cast the net and kill nations without sparing them. The later woe charges the despoiling of many nations and bloodshed, then promises the remaining peoples will despoil the aggressor. The later accusation and reversal answer the earlier portrayal of unchecked harm.
triples.source_text: Therefore they will cast their casting net and will not spare nations from continual killing.

target_units.text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

triples.relationship: prophetic waiting represented by a watcher's station
triples.rationale: Habakkuk stands at his watch to look for what God will speak. Isaiah likewise receives an instruction to station a watcher, who stands day and night and reports what is seen and heard from the Lord. Both use the watcher's position for attentive reception of a message.
triples.source_text: I will stand at my watch and step onto a rock; I will look out to see what He will speak within me and what I shall answer concerning my reproof.

target_units.text: For thus the Lord said to me: “Go, station a watcher for yourself, and report whatever you see.
I saw mounted riders, two horsemen, a donkey rider and a camel rider. Listen with great attention,
and call Uriah to the Lord’s watchtower.” He said, “I stood continually by day, and at the camp I stood all night,
and behold, he himself comes, a rider of a two-horse team.” He answered and said, “Babylon has fallen, and all her statues and handmade objects were shattered to the ground.”
Hear, you who remain and suffer; hear what I heard from the Lord Sabaoth. Israel’s God announced it to us.

triples.relationship: a prophetic message committed to a tablet
triples.rationale: Habakkuk is commanded to write the vision clearly on a boxwood tablet for its readers. Isaiah likewise is commanded to write on a tablet and in a book so that the words endure. Both explicitly require a written record, with different stated purposes and materials.
triples.source_text: The Lord answered me: “Write a vision clearly on a boxwood tablet, so that the one reading these things may pursue them.

target_units.text: Now then, sit and write these things on a tablet and in a book, because these things will endure for days of appointed times and for ever.

triples.relationship: later use of the coming-one promise to encourage endurance
triples.rationale: Habakkuk commands waiting if he delays because the coming one will come and not linger. Hebrews likewise urges endurance before repeating that the coming One will come and not delay. Both place the promise within an exhortation to patient expectation.
triples.source_text: For the vision is still for a season, and it will rise toward the end and not toward emptiness. If he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come and certainly will not linger.

target_units.text: For you need endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise.
“For yet a very little while, the coming One will come and will not delay.

triples.relationship: later quotation joining righteous life and the danger of drawing back
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says God's soul takes no pleasure in one drawing back and that the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Hebrews repeats both clauses in reversed order, saying My righteous one lives by faith. The connection preserves the distinct placement of My and the native faithfulness wording.
triples.source_text: If he draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him; but the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness.

target_units.text: But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he draws back, My soul takes no pleasure in him.”
But we are not people who draw back to destruction, but people of faith for the preservation of the soul.

triples.relationship: explicit later use of the righteous-one life statement
triples.rationale: Habakkuk declares that the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Romans introduces Scripture saying the righteous one lives by faith within its account of the gospel and God's righteousness. The shared statement is direct, while Habakkuk's possessive and faithfulness wording remain distinct.
triples.source_text: If he draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him; but the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness.

target_units.text: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written, “But the righteous one will live by faith.”

triples.relationship: later use of the righteous-one statement in discussion of law and faith
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Galatians quotes the righteous one living by faith while arguing about justification before God and law. The later argumentative use is recorded without silently replacing the source's My faithfulness wording.
triples.source_text: If he draws back, My soul has no pleasure in him; but the righteous one shall live by My faithfulness.

target_units.text: For all who are of works of law are under a curse, for it is written, “Accursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.”
Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by law, because “The righteous one will live by faith.”
But the law is not of faith; rather, “The one who does these things will live by them.”

triples.relationship: insatiable human appetite compared to Hades
triples.rationale: Habakkuk portrays the boastful conqueror's appetite as Hades and death, never filled despite gathered peoples. Proverbs likewise says Hades and destruction are not filled and compares them with insatiable human eyes. Both expressly link human insatiability with Hades.
triples.source_text: But the wine-soaked, contemptuous, boastful man will accomplish nothing. He widened his appetite like Hades and is like death, never filled; he will gather all nations and receive all peoples to himself.

target_units.text: Hades and destruction are not filled, and likewise human eyes are insatiable.

triples.relationship: a saying taken up against an oppressive ruler
triples.rationale: Habakkuk announces a parable and riddle taken up against one accumulating what is not his. Isaiah likewise introduces a lament against Babylon's king after release from harsh slavery and describes the taskmaster's end. Both turn the oppressor into the subject of a public saying after exploitation.
triples.source_text: Will not all these take up a parable against him and a riddle for his account? They will say, ‘Woe to the one multiplying for himself what is not his—how long?—and heavily weighting his collar!’

target_units.text: On that day God will give you rest from pain, your wrath and the harsh slavery in which you served them,
and you will take up this lament against Babylon’s king and say on that day, “How the one who made demands has rested, and the taskmaster rested!
God shattered the sinners’ yoke, the rulers’ yoke;
having struck a nation in wrath with an incurable blow, striking a nation with a blow of anger that did not spare,
he rested confidently. The whole earth cries out with gladness,

triples.relationship: same-chapter plunder threatened and explained as reversal
triples.rationale: Habakkuk 2:7 tells the addressed oppressor that he will become plunder when adversaries rise. The following verse explains that remaining peoples will despoil him because he despoiled many nations. The next unit gives the explicit reciprocal reason for the threatened loss.
triples.source_text: For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.

target_units.text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

triples.relationship: recompense corresponding to harm done to others
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says the despoiler of many nations will himself be despoiled by remaining peoples. Obadiah likewise announces that what was done will return upon the doer's own head. Both explicitly state reciprocal judgment, with Habakkuk specifying plunder and bloodshed.
triples.source_text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

triples.relationship: a high nest imagined as security from danger
triples.rationale: Habakkuk condemns setting a nest high to escape evils while acquiring evil gain. Obadiah likewise describes a high dwelling, imagined security from being brought down and a nest among stars from which God will bring its occupant down. Both challenge safety sought through elevated habitation.
triples.source_text: O you who acquire evil gain for your house, setting your nest on high to escape the hand of evils!

target_units.text: The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who camp in holes in the rocks, raising his dwelling high and saying in his heart, “Who will bring me down to the ground?”
If you soar like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.

triples.relationship: a house established through wrongdoing becomes an accusation
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says the plot brought shame upon the house and involved the end of many peoples. Jeremiah likewise condemns a house built without righteousness, unpaid labor, greed and innocent blood. Both connect the household's apparent advancement with culpable harm.
triples.source_text: You planned shame for your house, brought many peoples to an end, and your soul sinned.

target_units.text: O you who build your house without righteousness and your upper rooms without judgment! He works through his neighbor without payment and will not give him his wages.
You built yourself a well-proportioned house, airy upper rooms set apart by windows, paneled with cedar and painted with red ocher.
Will you reign because you are provoked in Ahaz your father? They will not eat or drink. It was better for you to do judgment and good righteousness.
They did not know; they did not judge a case for the lowly or a case for the poor. Is this not your failing to know Me? says the Lord.
Behold, neither your eyes nor your heart are good; instead they are directed toward your greed, innocent blood to shed it, wrongdoing, and murder to commit it.

triples.relationship: stones given the role of crying out
triples.rationale: Habakkuk depicts a stone crying from a wall and a beetle from wood uttering words. Jesus likewise says that stones will cry out if the disciples fall silent. The personified stone's speech is shared; the settings differ, and no beam is substituted for Habakkuk's beetle.
triples.source_text: For a stone will cry from a wall, and a beetle from wood will utter these things.

target_units.text: And some of the Pharisees from the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, rebuke Thy disciples.”
And He answered, “I tell you, if these fall silent, the stones will cry out.”

triples.relationship: building a city with bloodshed and injustice
triples.rationale: Habakkuk condemns building a city with bloodshed and preparing it with injustices. Micah likewise addresses leaders who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices. The distinctive paired accusation directly connects the passages.
triples.source_text: Woe to the one building a city with bloodshed and preparing a city with injustices!

target_units.text: Hear these things now, leaders of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house, who abhor justice and twist all straight things,
you who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices!

triples.relationship: earth filled with knowledge of the Lord compared to covering waters
triples.rationale: Habakkuk announces the earth filled with knowing the Lord's glory as water covers. Isaiah likewise declares the whole earth filled with knowledge of the Lord as abundant water covers the seas. Both combine universal knowledge of God with the covering-water comparison.
triples.source_text: For the earth will be filled with knowing the Lord’s glory, as water will cover them.

target_units.text: And they will certainly do no harm, nor will they be able at all to destroy anyone upon My holy mountain; for the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.

triples.relationship: the cup of divine judgment passes to those who harmed others
triples.rationale: Habakkuk commands the aggressor to drink dishonor because the cup from the Lord's right hand has reached him. Isaiah describes the Lord's cup of anger taken from Jerusalem and thrown into its oppressors' hands. Both portray judgment through a cup reaching wrongdoers.
triples.source_text: Drink, you too, a fullness of dishonor instead of glory; be tossed and shaken! The cup of the Lord’s right hand has come around to you, and dishonor has gathered upon your glory.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, rise, Jerusalem, you who drank the cup of anger from the Lord’s hand. You drank out and emptied the cup of falling, the bowl of anger.
There was no one to comfort you among all your children you bore, and no one to take your hand among all your sons you raised.
These two confront you—who will grieve with you?—fall and crushing, famine and sword. Who will comfort you?
Your sons are helpless, sleeping at every way out like a half-boiled beet, full of the Lord’s anger, exhausted because of the Lord God.
Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.
Thus says the Lord God who judges His people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling, the bowl of anger. You will not drink it again.
I will throw it into the hands of those who wronged and humbled you, who told your soul, “Bend down, so we may pass.” You laid your back level with the earth, outside for passersby.’”

triples.relationship: same-chapter repeated indictment for bloodshed and impiety
triples.rationale: Both units expressly accuse the addressed power of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all inhabitants. The repeated charge connects the woes while 2:17 also names Lebanon and wild animals, details absent from 2:8.
triples.source_text: For Lebanon’s impiety will cover you, and the misery of wild animals will terrify you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

target_units.text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

triples.relationship: the futility of worshiping objects made by their worshipers
triples.rationale: Habakkuk questions the use of carved and cast objects and the maker's trust in mute idols. Isaiah likewise calls fashioned gods useless and narrates a craftsman making an image from wood and worshiping it. Both expose reliance on human fabrication.
triples.source_text: What use is a carved image, that they carved it? They formed it as a cast object, a false appearance, because its maker trusted his creation, making mute idols.

target_units.text: All who fashion and carve are futile, making what pleases them, things that will not help them. But they will be ashamed—
all who fashion a god and carve useless things,
and all from whom they came have dried up. Let the deaf from among humankind all assemble and stand together; let them be abashed and ashamed together.
For a craftsman sharpened iron, worked it with an adze, bored it with a drill, and worked it with his strong arm. He will hunger and grow weak and certainly not drink water. Having selected
wood, a craftsman set it by measure and arranged it with glue. He made it like a man’s form and human beauty, to set it in a house.
The wood he cut from the woodland was what the Lord planted and rain made grow,
so that it might serve people for burning. Taking some, he warmed himself; after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. They worked the rest into gods and worship them.

Half of it they burned in fire, and after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. Over it he roasted meat, ate, and was satisfied. Warmed, he said, ‘It is pleasant for me, for I am warm and have seen fire!’
He made the rest into a carved god and worships it and prays, saying, ‘Rescue me, for you are my god.’

triples.relationship: wood adorned with precious metal cannot act as a living being
triples.rationale: Habakkuk mocks calling wood to wake and stone to rise, describing a gold-and-silver plate with no breath. Jeremiah likewise describes worked wood adorned with gold and silver, unable to move or take a step. Both oppose the decorated object to the powers expected of life.
triples.source_text: Woe to the one saying to wood, ‘Wake and rise!’ and to stone, ‘Be lifted up!’ It is an appearance, a plate of gold and silver, and no breath at all is in it.

target_units.text: For the nations’ customs are futile: it is wood cut from the woodland, a carpenter’s work and a cast object.
They are adorned with silver and gold; with hammers and nails they fastened them, and they will not move.
They must be lifted and carried, because they will not take a step. Do not fear them, because they certainly will not do evil, and no good is in them.

triples.relationship: cast images have no living spirit
triples.rationale: Habakkuk explicitly says the decorated image has no breath at all. Jeremiah likewise says cast objects are false and have no spirit in them, then calls them futile works that perish. Both deny life to the fabricated object.
triples.source_text: Woe to the one saying to wood, ‘Wake and rise!’ and to stone, ‘Be lifted up!’ It is an appearance, a plate of gold and silver, and no breath at all is in it.

target_units.text: Every human became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was put to shame at his carved things, because they cast false things; there is no spirit in them.
They are futile, mocked works; at the time of their visitation they will perish.

triples.relationship: the Lord located in His holy sanctuary
triples.rationale: Habakkuk contrasts mute idols with the Lord in His holy sanctuary. The psalm likewise places the Lord in His holy temple, with His throne in heaven and eyes examining people. Both explicitly identify His holy dwelling, while Habakkuk calls the earth to reverence.
triples.source_text: But the Lord is in His holy sanctuary; let all the earth revere Him.”

target_units.text: The Lord is in His holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven. His eyes look toward the needy; His eyelids examine the sons of men.

triples.relationship: mercy remembered in the face of divine wrath
triples.rationale: Habakkuk declares that God will remember mercy in wrath when his soul is troubled. The psalm likewise asks whether God will forget pity or shut His compassions in wrath, then recalls the Lord's works. This connection concerns mercy and wrath, without interpreting the two living creatures.
triples.source_text: Lord, I have heard Thy report and was afraid; I considered Thy works and was astonished. In the midst of two living creatures Thou wilt be known; when the years draw near Thou wilt be recognized; when the season arrives Thou wilt be revealed. When my soul is troubled, in wrath Thou wilt remember mercy.

target_units.text: “Will the Lord reject for the ages, and not again take pleasure?
Or will He cut off His mercy to the end, from generation to generation?
Or will God forget to show pity, or hold His compassions shut in His wrath?” Diapsalma.
And I said, “Now I have begun; this is the change of the Most High’s right hand.”
I remembered the Lord’s works, for I will remember Thy wonders from the beginning,

triples.relationship: divine appearance described as coming from a mountain region
triples.rationale: Habakkuk depicts God coming from Teman and the Holy One from a shaded mountain, with excellence covering heaven. Deuteronomy likewise describes the Lord coming from Sinai, appearing from Seir and hastening from Mount Paran. The mountain-coming pattern is shared without equating the named locations.
triples.source_text: God will come from Teman, the Holy One from a mountain shaded and thickly wooded. Diapsalma. His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth is full of His praise.

target_units.text: And he said, The Lord has come from Sinai, and appeared unto us from Seir, and hastened from Mount Paran with myriads of Kadesh; at His right hand were angels with Him.
And He spared His people; and all the consecrated ones are under Thy hands; and these are under Thee; and the people received from His words

triples.relationship: brightness in the description of divine glory
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes divine brightness like light, followed by horns in His hands and mighty love. Ezekiel likewise depicts brightness around the visible likeness of the Lord's glory, comparing it to a bow in cloud. The link concerns radiance, without treating the other visionary details as identical.
triples.source_text: His brightness will be like light; horns are in His hands, and He established mighty love of His strength.

target_units.text: I saw something like the sight of electrum from the appearance of a waist upward; and from the appearance of a waist down below I saw something like the appearance of fire, with its brightness all around.

Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

triples.relationship: earth and mountains shaken and peoples melted before God
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes the earth shaking, nations melting and mountains crushed. Nahum likewise depicts mountains and earth shaken, rulers melted by fury and rocks crushed. Both present divine presence through these combined images of shaking, melting and crushing.
triples.source_text: He stood, and the earth shook; He looked, and nations melted. Mountains were crushed violently; everlasting hills melted.

target_units.text: Mountains shook before Him and hills were shaken; the whole earth recoiled before Him, and all who dwell in it.
Who will stand before His anger? Who will resist His furious wrath? His fury melts rulers, and rocks were crushed before Him.

triples.relationship: terror and flight in Midian's camp
triples.rationale: Habakkuk says the tents of Midian will be terrified. Judges narrates panic and flight in the camp identified earlier as Midian's, with the Lord setting swords against neighbors. The narrative supplies a particular example of Midianite camp terror, without asserting that Habakkuk identifies this event exclusively.
triples.source_text: I saw His everlasting journeys in place of toils; the dwellings of Ethiopians will be terrified, and the tents of the land of Midian.

target_units.text: Gideon and the hundred men with him entered a section of the camp as the middle watch began. He thoroughly roused the guards, and they sounded the horn trumpets and dashed the jars in their hands.

The three companies sounded the horn trumpets and shattered the jars. They grasped the torches in their left hands, with the horn trumpets in their right hands to sound them, and cried, “A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!”
Each stood by himself around the camp. The whole camp ran; they sounded the alarm and fled.

The three hundred horn trumpets sounded, and the Lord set each man’s sword against his neighbour throughout the camp. The camp fled as far as Beth-shittah and, gathered together, as far as the edge of Abel-meholah and toward Tabbath.

triples.relationship: salvation associated with God's passage through waters
triples.rationale: Habakkuk questions fury against rivers and sea and calls God's riding salvation. The psalm recalls the redemption of His people, fearful waters and depths, and His way in the sea. Both combine divine passage through waters with the people's deliverance.
triples.source_text: Wast Thou angry with rivers, Lord? Was Thy fury against rivers, or Thine onrush against the sea, that Thou wilt mount Thy horses and Thy riding is salvation?

target_units.text: With Thine arm Thou didst redeem Thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Diapsalma.
The waters saw Thee, God; the waters saw Thee and feared, and the depths were troubled—a multitude of sounding waters.
The clouds gave voice, for Thine arrows too pass through.
Thy thunder’s voice was in the wheel; Thy flashes of lightning shone upon the inhabited world; the earth shook and became trembling.
Thy way is in the sea, and Thy paths in many waters, and Thy tracks will not be known.

triples.relationship: God depicted bending a bow for judgment
triples.rationale: Habakkuk pictures God bending His bow against scepters. The psalm likewise presents God as righteous judge and describes Him bending a bow and preparing deadly arrows. The martial image portrays divine judgment, with different objects specified.
triples.source_text: Thou wilt surely bend Thy bow against scepters, says the Lord. Diapsalma. The earth will be torn apart by rivers.

target_units.text: God is a righteous judge, strong and patient, not bringing wrath every day.
If you do not return, He will polish His sword; He bent His bow and prepared it,
and in it He prepared instruments of death; He fashioned His arrows for those being burned.

triples.relationship: waters and depths described with sound during divine appearance
triples.rationale: Habakkuk combines peoples' travail, scattered waters and the abyss giving voice in God's passage. The psalm likewise portrays waters seeing God in fear, troubled depths, sounding waters and clouds giving voice. Both animate the waters in the depiction of divine appearance.
triples.source_text: Peoples will see Thee and travail, as He scatters waters in His passage. The abyss gave its voice, the height of its appearance.

target_units.text: The waters saw Thee, God; the waters saw Thee and feared, and the depths were troubled—a multitude of sounding waters.
The clouds gave voice, for Thine arrows too pass through.
Thy thunder’s voice was in the wheel; Thy flashes of lightning shone upon the inhabited world; the earth shook and became trembling.

triples.relationship: sun and moon within an account of divine battle
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes the sun raised, the moon standing in its appointed place and bright weapons. Joshua's battle account likewise names the sun standing and the moon remaining still while the Lord fights for Israel. The common celestial and battle setting is retained, while Habakkuk's sun-raised wording is not changed.
triples.source_text: The sun was raised, and the moon stood in its appointed place. Thy missiles will go into light, into the brightness of Thy flashing weapons.

target_units.text: Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day God handed the Amorites over to Israel, when He crushed them at Gibeon and they were crushed before the sons of Israel. Joshua said, “Let the sun stand over Gibeon, and the moon over the ravine of Aijalon.”
The sun stood, and the moon remained still, until God repelled their enemies. The sun stood in the middle of heaven and did not advance toward sunset for a full day.
There was no such day before or afterward, when God listened to a human being, for the Lord fought alongside Israel.

triples.relationship: divine fury directed against nations
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes nations brought down in divine fury and earth diminished by threat. Isaiah likewise summons nations and earth to hear because the Lord's wrath and anger are against nations to hand them to slaughter. Both explicitly connect judgment upon nations with divine fury.
triples.source_text: With threat Thou wilt diminish the earth, and in fury Thou wilt bring nations down.

target_units.text: Draw near, nations, and hear, rulers! Let the earth and those in it hear, the inhabited world and the people in it!
For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.

triples.relationship: salvation and mercy for God's anointed
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes God going out to save His people and His anointed ones. The psalm likewise magnifies His king's salvations and mercy to His anointed, David and his seed. The connection preserves the source's plural anointed ones and the psalm's specifically named royal recipient.
triples.source_text: Thou didst go out for Thy people’s salvation, to save Thine anointed ones. Thou didst cast death upon the heads of lawless people and didst raise bonds up to the neck. Diapsalma.

target_units.text: magnifying the salvations of His king and showing mercy to His anointed, to David and to his seed for ever.

triples.relationship: God's way through the sea's waters
triples.rationale: Habakkuk pictures God's horses driven into the sea and troubling much water. The psalm likewise describes God's way in the sea and paths in many waters. Both portray divine movement through water, without assigning horses to the psalm.
triples.source_text: Thou didst drive Thy horses into the sea as they troubled much water.

target_units.text: Thy way is in the sea, and Thy paths in many waters, and Thy tracks will not be known.

triples.relationship: bodily distress in response to a prophetic encounter
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes terror in his belly, trembling in his bones and a troubled bodily condition. Daniel likewise describes strong fear surrounding the vision and his own loss of strength and fall to the ground. Both describe the bodily effect of the encounter, with distinct sensations and accounts of sound.
triples.source_text: I kept watch, and my belly was terrified at the sound of the prayer of my lips. Trembling entered my bones, and my bodily condition beneath me was troubled. I will rest on a day of affliction, to go up to the people of my sojourning.

target_units.text: I, Daniel, saw this great vision, but the men with me did not see it. Strong fear fell upon them, and they fled in haste.
I was left alone and saw this great vision. No strength remained in me; a spirit turned upon me for destruction, and I had no strength.
I did not hear the sound of his speech; I had fallen face down upon the earth.

triples.relationship: failure of fields, vines and fig trees
triples.rationale: Habakkuk lists failed figs, vines, olives and fields producing no food. Joel likewise describes failed grain, diminished oil and dried or diminished vines, figs and field trees. Both enumerate agricultural loss across several crops.
triples.source_text: For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and vines will have no produce; the olive’s labor will fail, and fields will not produce food. Sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no cattle at feeding troughs.

target_units.text: because the plains have suffered. Let the earth mourn, because grain has suffered, wine has dried up, and oil has diminished.
The farmers have dried up. Lament, estates, over wheat and barley, because the harvest from the field has perished.
The vine has dried up and the fig trees have diminished; pomegranate, palm, apple tree and all the field’s trees have dried up, because human beings have put joy to shame.

triples.relationship: cattle and sheep without food
triples.rationale: Habakkuk describes sheep failing for lack of food and no cattle at feeding troughs. Joel likewise says cattle have no pasture and sheep disappeared. The animals' food failure is a distinct shared element of the agricultural calamity.
triples.source_text: For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and vines will have no produce; the olive’s labor will fail, and fields will not produce food. Sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no cattle at feeding troughs.

target_units.text: What shall we store up for ourselves? Herds of cattle wept because they had no pasture, and flocks of sheep disappeared.

triples.relationship: rejoicing in God as Savior
triples.rationale: Habakkuk declares that he will exult in the Lord and rejoice in God his Savior. Mary's song likewise magnifies the Lord and says her spirit rejoiced in God her Savior. The closely corresponding declaration links the two songs.
triples.source_text: But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in God my Savior.

target_units.text: Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior,

triples.relationship: God's strength places the speaker's feet upon heights
triples.rationale: Habakkuk names God as his strength, setting his feet toward completion and leading him onto heights. The psalm likewise describes divine power, a blameless way, firmly set feet and standing on heights. The shared cluster is retained without importing the psalm's deer comparison into Habakkuk.
triples.source_text: The Lord God is my strength; He will set my feet toward completion and lead me onto the heights, to conquer in His song.

target_units.text: God girds me with power and made my way blameless,
He sets my feet firmly like a deer’s and makes me stand upon the heights,
training my hands for war; and Thou madest my arms a bronze bow.

deferred_source_units.reason: The complete oracle heading naming Habakkuk was read. No sufficiently particular target was retained for this heading alone; generic prophetic headings were not counted merely for sharing a form.

deferred_source_units.source_text: Are these things not from the Lord Almighty? Many peoples failed in fire, and many nations lost heart.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: Are these things not from the Lord Almighty? Many peoples failed in fire, and many nations lost heart.
unresolved_candidates.reason: The supplied Jeremiah text burns Babylon's gates but says peoples will not labor in vain and nations perish at the beginning. It does not contain the proposed nations-laboring-for-fire wording. The particular claimed parallel was not retained by substituting another translation.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Babylon’s wall was broadened; it will be utterly demolished, and her high gates burned. Peoples will not labor in vain, and nations will perish at the beginning.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: O you who make your neighbor drink with a turbid overthrow and intoxicate him, so that you may look upon their caves!
unresolved_candidates.reason: Genesis explicitly describes Noah's drunkenness and exposed nakedness, whereas Habakkuk describes intoxicating a neighbor in order to look upon caves. The native object differs, so the proposed exposure connection was not accepted.

target_units.text: And he drank of the wine and became drunk, and lay uncovered in his house.
And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness, and went out and told his two brothers outside.

And Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it across their shoulders, and walked backward to cover their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s nakedness.
